title: Carbon leakage

definition.text: A rise in greenhouse gas emissions in one country caused by another country cutting its own emissions under stricter climate policies.

facts.text: The leakage rate is the rise in emissions outside the acting countries divided by the cut inside them, as a percentage that can exceed 100%.
A rate above 100% would mean domestic action actually increased global emissions.
Leakage happens when climate policy raises local costs, so production moves to countries with laxer rules while demand stays the same.
It can also happen through fuel markets: lower demand cuts fuel prices, and countries without a carbon price use more.
Estimates for action under the Kyoto Protocol ranged from 5 to 20%, but were seen as very uncertain; there is no consensus on long-term leakage.
The EU gives free ETS allowances to sectors at high risk of leakage, such as aluminium, using a Carbon Leakage Indicator of trade intensity times emission intensity.
Firm-level evidence found the EU ETS cut regulated manufacturers' CO₂ emissions by 14–16% with no observed carbon leakage.

contested_note: Sources say there is no consensus on how large long-term carbon leakage is.

definition.text: A market-based way of controlling pollution in which a government caps total emissions and issues permits that polluters can buy and sell.

facts.text: Also called cap and trade, it is used for carbon dioxide and other greenhouse gases as well as sulfur dioxide and other pollutants.
Polluters must hold permits equal to their emissions; one that wants to emit more must buy permits from others willing to sell.
In effect the buyer pays a charge for polluting, while the seller is rewarded for cutting its emissions.
Its goal is to meet a set emissions target at the lowest cost, letting firms decide how to meet it, unlike command-and-control rules.
Some schemes let participants bank allowances for later periods, which lets them cut emissions when it is most efficient.
Usually the government lowers the overall limit over time towards a national reduction target.
A 2024 meta-analysis of 80 evaluations across 21 carbon-pricing systems found average emission cuts of about 5–21% (around 4–15% after correcting for publication bias).

definition.text: The idea that trading permits makes pollution cuts happen first wherever they are cheapest, so a target is met at the lowest total cost.

facts.text: Each polluter chooses between buying or selling permits, installing cleaner technology or cutting output, depending on its marginal abatement cost and the permit price.
In theory this spreads reductions efficiently among polluters and lowers compliance costs compared with command-and-control rules.
In a Lagrange optimization of the least-cost target, the Lagrange multiplier plays the role of the market permit price.
This is a version of the equi-marginal principle used in economics to find the most efficient decision.
Coase (1960) argued social costs could be handled by negotiating property rights, assuming perfect markets and equal bargaining power.

definition.text: The development of cap and trade from computer studies of air pollution costs in the late 1960s to national and global carbon markets.

facts.text: Simulation studies between 1967 and 1970 found that a least-cost solution was dramatically cheaper than conventional abatement strategies.
The 1977 Clean Air Act took up an offset mechanism: a firm could emit more if it paid another firm to cut the same pollutant.
The first cap-and-trade system was the US Acid Rain Program under the 1990 Clean Air Act, announced as a paradigm shift in environmental policy.
The approach then spread from US clean air policy to global climate policy and the European Union.

title: Prices versus quantities
article: Emissions trading#Prices versus quantities, and the safety valve

definition.text: The long-running debate over whether pollution is better controlled by fixing its price, as a tax does, or fixing its quantity, as a cap does.

facts.text: With a cap, uncertain supply and demand make permit prices uncertain, and industry bears the cost of that volatility.
A tax's main drawback is that the environmental outcome, such as a limit on emissions, is not guaranteed.
Under a uniform tax the agency cannot pick winners and losers, which leaves less room for corruption.
A tax sets a unit price and the market sets the quantity; under cap and trade the authorities set the quantity and the market sets the price.
Cap and trade adjusts to inflation automatically and its price falls in recessions, acting as an automatic stabilizer.
Under uncertainty it is not clear which instrument is more efficient.

contested_note: Economists have long disagreed on whether price or quantity instruments are better for cutting emissions.

title: Safety valve (emissions trading)
article: Emissions trading#Prices versus quantities, and the safety valve

definition.text: A hybrid of a cap and a tax: a cap-and-trade system in which the permit price is held below a maximum, or above a minimum.

facts.text: Emitters can buy permits on the market or from the government at a set trigger price.
Setting the trigger price high enough, or the permits few enough, lets it mimic a pure quantity or pure price instrument.
A price ceiling removes the certainty of a fixed emissions limit.
A price floor gives certainty for investment in cutting emissions, which matters when cuts are urgent.

definition.text: A trading scheme in which polluters earn credits, or offsets, by cutting emissions below a baseline, often their historical emissions.

facts.text: The credits can be bought by polluters that face a regulatory limit.
Credit programmes usually require additionality: cutting more than existing rules already demand.
Additionality is hard to define and monitor; some companies deliberately raised emissions in order to be paid to remove them.

definition.text: Separate cap-and-trade systems joined together by recognising each other's allowances for compliance.

facts.text: Linking makes a larger carbon market, which can lower compliance costs, raise liquidity and stabilise prices.
Some scholars see linking as a bottom-up starting point for international climate policy.
California and Québec linked their systems in 2014; the EU ETS has linked with Switzerland's system.

definition.text: Markets in licences that give the right to raise pollution at a given location by no more than a set amount, rather than the right to emit a set amount.

facts.text: Pollution at each location is modelled as a linear combination of emissions through a diffusion matrix H, with q=H⋅e.
A polluter that affects several monitoring points must hold a portfolio of licences covering all of them.
Montgomery showed both markets allocate licences efficiently, but pollution-licence markets apply more widely.

title: EU Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism

definition.text: A European Union carbon tariff on carbon-intensive imports such as steel, cement and some electricity.

facts.text: Its main aim is to stop carbon leakage by charging covered imports the same carbon price as EU producers pay under the EU ETS.
Importers must buy CBAM certificates, priced in line with EU ETS allowances, to cover the emissions embedded in their goods.
It covers aluminium, cement, electricity, fertilisers, hydrogen and iron and steel, with reporting from October 2023 and payment from 2026.
Free EU ETS allowances in the covered sectors will be phased out by 2034.
It may push other countries to adopt carbon pricing; Brazil, Indonesia, Taiwan, Vietnam, Malaysia and Serbia are doing so partly because of it.
Some see it as the start of a climate club of the kind William Nordhaus proposed.
An Asian Development Bank report says it will cut emissions only a little while harming imports to the EU.
Questions remain over its compatibility with WTO rules and its effect on least developed countries.

contested_note: Supporters call it a key fix for carbon leakage, while critics say it does little for emissions, burdens EU firms and may clash with trade rules.
